axes.brief: The presidency dominates national policy and genuine competition, legislative scrutiny and judicial independence are severely constrained. Elections and civilian constitutional offices remain in place, which does not imply either expert-panel rule or military appointment.
axes.counterEvidence: Formal adult suffrage, legislative lawmaking, no-confidence/impeachment procedures and legally binding referendums coexist with systematic obstacles to their independent use. These distinctions moderate several answers.

answers.rationale: Inference from managed elections and exclusion of genuine challengers: remaining in office does not require winning free competitive contests.
The constitutional selection mechanism is presidential election and presidential/parliamentary appointment of ministers, not an expert panel choosing national government.

Article 32 gives adult citizens voting rights without education or IQ qualifications, subject to incapacity and imprisonment exclusions; electoral manipulation concerns meaningful choice rather than an educational franchise.

Presidential decrees provide extensive executive lawmaking but Article 90 forbids contradicting federal law and federal statutes formally require parliament. Dominance over parliament and these retained legal limits support a mixed inference.
Opposition figures and organisations face disqualification, imprisonment and extremist designations, while incumbent access to state resources prevents equal campaigning conditions.

Nominal parliamentary oversight does not give independent opposition an effective ability to investigate presidential spending; legislative subordination and repression of anti-corruption investigators point against the proposition.
Constitutional adjudication exists, but politically subordinate courts cannot independently overturn the executive in the sense this statement requires.
Neither constitutional appointment rules nor actual presidential dominance give trade-union leaders authority to select national government.
Extremism and related political exclusion rules are used against genuine challengers, evidencing leadership control over the range of permitted parties and positions.

The referendum law permits citizen initiative and binding normative decisions, including revisiting legislation within subject exclusions. High procedural hurdles and executive control limit its practical availability; this is a legally present but politically constrained mechanism.
The concentrated presidential system and subordinate parliament give the incumbent decisive practical control of major national policy, beyond ordinary executive leadership.

Articles 93 and 117 retain impeachment/no-confidence procedures, but political subordination makes removal for executive abuse practically ineffective. Formal accountability and actual insulation pull in opposite directions.

Emergency-election law assigns decisions to the election commission after security consultations; presidential domination does not establish the exact unilateral postponement power for political continuity asked here. Independent approval in practice is insufficiently evidenced.

National constitutional institutions provide fixed parliamentary terms and removal procedures, not a national voter-initiated recall mechanism; local recall provisions do not establish this national accountability right.
Managed elections, controlled legislature and repression of challengers insulate the executive from effective voter or representative accountability.

The president is civilian commander-in-chief under Article 87. The institutional hierarchy does not authorise armed forces to judge and replace civilian government. Militarisation is not a military right of removal.

axes.brief: Criminalised dissent, intrusive communications rules and broad security powers favour state control. Literal legal safeguards and distinctions between firearm classes or random stops and mandatory testing are assessed separately.
axes.counterEvidence: Courts remain formally necessary for detention and many searches; licensed self-defence weapons are available. Judicial dependence weakens safeguards but does not justify inventing unlimited detention powers.

answers.rationale: Non-prescribed drug use is itself an administrative offence under Article 6.9, even without a separate victim. Treatment exemptions do not create adult freedom to use drugs.
Article 23 allows court-authorised interception; the security apparatus also has extensive access. The narrower serious-crime power in the question is clearly accepted.
Public assembly is subject to restrictive approvals and peaceful antiwar protest is punished; temporary obstruction does not enjoy the proposed protected status.
Army-discrediting prosecutions and punishment for peaceful opposition show that offensive institutional criticism is not protected merely because it is criticism.

Compulsory treatment is available for severe mental disorder posing danger to the person themself under the psychiatric-care law; this supports a qualified self-protective health power, not unrestricted treatment of competent adults.
Long communications retention and migrant geolocation monitoring establish surveillance, but the reviewed material does not establish several-year retention of ordinary nonsuspects’ movement records.
Traffic stops may be broad, but compulsory intoxication testing requires statutory grounds to suspect impairment. Random stopping is not permission for suspicion-free testing.

Involuntary psychiatric hospitalisation can continue with judicial review where a serious disorder creates immediate danger to others before an offence. This is a defined preventive-health power, not unrestricted preventive detention.
Film and online-content restrictions expressly protect traditional values, alongside bans on LGBT information; adult access is not generally protected against official moral objections.

Messenger operators must identify users through telephone subscribers, with retained information accessible to authorities; this state-mandated identity infrastructure contradicts unrestricted anonymous use.
Counterterrorism zones permit identity checks and searches of entrants and vehicles without individualised criminal suspicion. The credible-area-threat case is accepted.
Authorities possess powers to restrict assemblies on public-order/security grounds and use broader restrictions in practice; credible serious disorder plainly qualifies.
The default warrant rule has urgency exceptions including threatened loss of evidence, and counterterrorism zones allow entry. These exceed the question’s sole immediate-safety exception.

Security-secret and antiwar prosecutions lack a general misconduct-disclosure exemption; investigative reporting about official abuses is punished rather than protected by the proposed public-interest right.

Article 13 permits licensed civilian smoothbore self-defence and limited-lethality firearms with disqualifications and training. Restrictions on ordinary handguns and carrying qualify, but do not erase, legal defensive ownership.

The constitution requires a court decision beyond 48 hours, while political dependence undermines genuinely independent review. Sources do not establish open-ended terrorism detention until authorities declare the threat resolved; neither formal review alone nor abuse proves this exact proposition.

axes.brief: Federal policy prioritises a Russian-language shared civic identity and migrants’ adaptation to established national values. It simultaneously recognises indigenous and constituent peoples’ languages and traditions, so national unity is not equivalent to cultural uniformity.
axes.counterEvidence: The 2026 nationalities programme funds minority culture and language activity; regional religious holidays remain possible. These accommodations qualify assimilation in service, identity and calendar questions.

answers.rationale: Migration policy places national security and integration into Russian traditional values ahead of maintaining conflicting migrant customs.

State programmes finance ethno-cultural and language institutions, but migrants face Russian-language school and integration conditions. Accommodation receives public funds within a shared-language framework.
The migration concept expects sociocultural adaptation and respect for Russian traditions as conditions of successful permanent integration.
The nationalities strategy recognises ethnic and linguistic diversity within a common civic nation; a distinct cultural identity is permissible provided it does not displace civic unity.
Russian is the nationwide state language and 2026 consumer-information rules require Russian; foreign-language duplication is conditional rather than equivalent institutional priority.

Presidential decree 799 created a national observance for Indigenous small-numbered peoples, first celebrated on 30 April 2026 with documented cultural and commemorative ceremonies. This supports public acknowledgement without prescribing a formula for every national ceremony.

Values policy gives Russian culture and Orthodoxy special historical weight, while the implemented nationalities framework also funds many peoples’ traditions. Mixed priority is more supportable than an unverified majority share of cultural spending.

The nationalities strategy makes common civic identity and territorial unity overarching principles. Distinct identity is protected within that framework rather than given precedence when it conflicts.
A federal calendar coexists with legally permitted regional religious holidays, including Muslim holidays. Russia does not enforce only one common cultural calendar everywhere.
The constitution’s multinational people and 2026 strategy explicitly recognise the cultural heritage of multiple constituent peoples.
Migration policy expressly calls for sociocultural adaptation and integration into the wider Russian community, while opposing isolation and security risks.

Public-facing information must be Russian; other languages may duplicate it under legal conditions. Permitting duplication is weaker than a policy requiring foreign-language signage for migrant communities.
Values and civic-identity policy encourages intergenerational attachment to the common nation while allowing ethnic identities. This is a qualified priority, not a demand to erase family heritage.
Regional restrictions and religious discussions of face veils do not establish the exact exception requested: legality when other full-body coverings are prohibited.
The strategy explicitly includes different peoples’ ways of life and ethnic cultures within national identity, with indigenous cultural preservation programmes.
The migration programme stresses common language, norms and traditional Russian values as integration goals rather than separate-community maintenance.

axes.brief: The state restricts entry and residence through quotas, registration, security checks, deportation and cultural integration. Compatriot, family, education, Eurasian labour and values-based exceptions prevent interpreting this as a universal skill-only or single numerical cap.
axes.counterEvidence: The 2026 quota concerns temporary residence and has extensive exceptions; permanent-resident foreigners can receive specified benefits. Refugee protection exists in law but permanent settlement is not universally guaranteed.

answers.rationale: The 2026 temporary-residence quota is restrictive and regionally allocated, but Article 8 and decree 702 provide uncapped exceptions. A strict annual cap on all permanent settlement is therefore only partly reflected.

Settlement requires a qualifying legal route, Russian-language/legal knowledge in ordinary cases and security compliance. Improving living conditions alone gives no general right, though multiple non-work routes exist.
Family, education, compatriot and values-based residence routes expressly admit people without economically important skills. Skill-only permanent eligibility contradicts the law.

Children of permanent residents have a direct residence route; spouses do not uniformly have the same entitlement, with privileged spousal routes often tied to Russian citizens or qualified-worker categories. Family joining is substantial but conditional.

Refugee and temporary-asylum recognition protect against persecution, but do not confer an unconditional permanent-settlement entitlement on every refugee. Separate status and residence procedures remain.
The controlled-persons register, removal powers and enforced regularisation deadlines favour deportation or compulsory status correction rather than allowing unauthorised migrants to remain.

Residence controls and the migration concept’s security/cultural requirements apply independently of employers’ recruitment preferences. Labour needs do not create an unrestricted permanent-admission right.
The concept rejects replacement migration and stresses security and adaptation; reviewed sources do not isolate the precise housing/public-service tradeoff against positive economic benefits.
Children and specified family categories receive quota-exempt residence; the temporary quota is not a common universal ceiling shared by all permanent and family immigration.

Employment permits and Eurasian routes admit many workers with jobs, while nationality, sector, permits and security conditions restrict others. A job offer facilitates entry but is not generally sufficient across applicants.
Independent education, compatriot and values-based routes do not require employer or family sponsorship, contradicting a universal sponsor requirement.

An accredited full-time honours degree provides a direct permanent-residence route under Article 8. The statement’s rejection of education-only routes is therefore contradicted, although ordinary graduation is not always sufficient.

The asylum system is legally separate from the ordinary temporary-residence quota and recognises persecution grounds. Serious implementation restrictions qualify this support without turning protection into a skill-based quota.

Policy prioritises compatriots and people sharing Russian traditional values. This supports cultural-affinity selection, though decree 702 can favour ideologically aligned applicants from otherwise culturally different countries.

Social Fund rules extend specified child, sickness and pension benefits to legally resident foreigners, refugees and insured foreign workers; eligibility varies by status rather than excluding all noncitizens.
Migration policy seeks integration, compatriot return and shared values; it does not seek additional cultural difference as an independent reason to increase admission.

axes.brief: Continuing the invasion of Ukraine, maintaining expeditionary forces, conscription and high-end weapons, and public military threats show strong reliance on force. The assessment does not adopt official claims that aggression is legally defensive.
axes.counterEvidence: Russia still conducts diplomacy and proposes reciprocal arms limits. Human-control statements and reports of AI capabilities do not by themselves settle whether each target may be attacked without approval.

answers.rationale: The continuing full-scale invasion of Ukraine demonstrates willingness to use force outside an actual attack on Russia; official defensive descriptions do not change the observed initiation of war.
Continuation of the war and coercive military pressure rather than accepting slower diplomatic resolution indicate that diplomacy does not take precedence when it conflicts with objectives.
Large-scale military mobilisation, costly weapons development and 2026 exercises demonstrate readiness to incur major costs for military advantage over potential opponents.

The foreign-policy concept permits armed force to protect national security within Russia’s expansive account of self-defence. Its approach supports the narrower imminent-attack case, without endorsing Russia’s legal justification for Ukraine.
Russia’s initiated and continuing war goes beyond responding to an armed attack on itself or an ally.
Male conscription remains compulsory for a year;2026 law expands conscription administration across the year while retaining designated dispatch periods.
Maintaining the war and territorial demands despite its costs supports reluctance to make substantial position-weakening concessions, though negotiations are not excluded altogether.

The Foreign Ministry endorses human control over AI weapons; it does not specify approval of every strike. AI weapon development and broad human-control assurances cannot resolve that exact autonomy threshold.
Sustained combat in Ukraine and forces able to project power abroad contradict a defence policy confined to repelling attacks.
Military partnership exercises and Russia’s use of force are incompatible with avoiding military action at all costs even to defend an ally.
The continuing multi-year campaign in Ukraine is direct evidence of maintaining forces for prolonged combat beyond Russia’s internationally recognised borders.
Russia has used war and annexation claims to change territorial control rather than leave the dispute unresolved. This describes conduct without recognising annexation.
Putin’s October 2026 threats concerning European conflict and military capabilities demonstrate willingness to use military threats in international disputes.
Military demonstrations and continued war despite escalation risks give forceful resolve priority over minimising war risk in the relevant conflicts.

NATO’s July 2026 attribution of persistent Russian military-linked cyber activity supports willingness to gather intelligence despite diplomatic consequences. This is an attributed operational assessment, not an admission by Moscow.

The adopted 2023 foreign-policy concept supports conditions for further phased nuclear reductions, while the 2026 position proposes reciprocal quantitative limits and actual policy continues military expansion. This is conditional support for negotiated reduction; a freeze alone is not treated as a new reduction.

axes.brief: Domestic constitutional supremacy and rejection of external human-rights constraints favour sovereignty. Russia nonetheless delegates real economic powers to the EAEU and shares programmes and security commitments with Belarus and other partners.
axes.counterEvidence: EAEU rules and courts, Union State programmes and alliance commitments are material counterevidence. Cooperation is selective and preserves national constitutional and monetary authority.

answers.rationale: Article 79 makes international-body decisions unenforceable when interpreted contrary to Russia’s constitution, reserving ultimate domestic constitutional authority.
EAEU bodies exercise delegated binding economic powers, but constitutional supremacy and rejection of unwanted external rulings limit the acceptance of adverse international decisions.
Constitutional supremacy over conflicting interpretations of international obligations gives domestic constitutional adjudication the final word.

Longstanding collective-security and Union State arrangements include coordinated defence and joint institutions, and 2026 joint exercises implement those commitments. Russia accepts selected alliance constraints.
Treaty termination law assigns decisions to the competent Russian organs, following treaty conditions and international law; it does not require an international institution’s political permission.

Russia participates in limited economic adjudication but rejects ICC authority over officials and adverse supranational human-rights enforcement. The question’s broad jurisdiction is therefore opposed, with treaty-specific exceptions.
Continuing the Ukraine war despite international condemnation and constitutional limits on external decisions show priority for asserted national interests over contrary institutional goals.

Participation in environmental cooperation does not establish willingness to delegate binding cross-border environmental decisions. No sufficiently specific institutional delegation or categorical refusal was verified.

Russia retains an independent foreign policy while implementing foreign/security coordination through the Union State. This is selective coordination, neither blanket exclusion from coordinating blocs nor a fully common external policy.
Constitutional resistance to adverse external rulings and repression of international rights organisations contradict a right for international human-rights institutions to require legal changes.
The constitution and Bank of Russia framework retain ruble issuance and monetary policy nationally; EAEU cooperation uses national currencies rather than a shared central bank.
Union State programmes and EAEU institutions pool funding and decisions in defined shared economic, technical and security matters. The delegation remains bounded.

Russia controls immigration and border security nationally but shares customs rules and labour-mobility obligations in the EAEU. The proposition’s sole-authority claim is therefore only partly reflected.
EAEU membership implements common customs and negotiated trade rules rather than setting every trade rule unilaterally.

Current institutions preserve Russian constitutional sovereignty within selective Union State integration; Russia has not transferred general national policy to a political federation. This is qualified by continuing joint governance.

Russia selectively supports collective rules but continues conduct in Ukraine condemned as violating them. This weighs against enforcement taking precedence when it sacrifices immediate state interests.

axes.brief: Russia combines widespread private business with state ownership in strategic energy, finance, transport and broadcasting. Selective privatisation continues alongside seizures and temporary administration, which are distinguished from permanent public ownership.
axes.counterEvidence: Private providers can participate in public medical insurance and state procurement. The 2026–2028 sale programme excludes natural monopolies and defence enterprises; foreign-firm administration does not prove a policy of public ownership for all commerce.

answers.rationale: Private commercial enterprise remains a normal economy-wide institution, and the federal programme sells nonstrategic holdings. Strategic state dominance qualifies support without showing that most individual businesses must be public.
Water law restricts disposal of public water networks and requires preservation of majority public control; Moscow’s major water company is wholly municipal.

Nonstrategic privatisation supports private provision, while legally protected public utility and strategic ownership persists independent of a simple price-quality test. Sector-specific policy is mixed.

State-controlled Gazprom and Sber operate in commercially contested sectors rather than leaving all competitive activity to private owners. This is support for selective public firms, not universal nationalisation.
The ministry maintains extensive public hospital and research-treatment institutions, with private insurance participants supplementing rather than replacing the public ownership model.
The current RZD charter retains the Russian Federation as owner of the railway company; the integrated national railway infrastructure is publicly owned.

Private providers can receive mandatory-insurance funding and public bodies purchase services competitively. This supports conditional contracting without a universal duty to outsource every cheaper service.
Sber remains majority owned by the Russian Federation while private banks operate alongside it. This directly implements the mixed banking ownership proposition.

The 2026–2028 programme sells selected commercial holdings but excludes defence and natural monopolies; strategic public control and temporary takeovers remain. Sale is selective rather than a general rule.
Public housing exists, but evidence reviewed does not establish the substantial-share preference for rental stock as a whole. Housing provision or mortgage subsidies alone would not answer ownership.
Defence enterprises and strategic monopolies are excluded from ordinary privatisation, showing ownership is used for security beyond regulation alone. Some security-related private firms remain.
Majority state control of Gazprom and the wider strategic-resource model support public resource ownership, qualified by substantial private extraction companies.

Competitive contracting and regional waste operators do not by themselves establish a preference for privately owned routine-service providers over municipal companies. Ownership-specific comparative evidence remains insufficient.
The privatisation programme expressly excludes defence and natural-monopoly enterprises, retaining strategic ownership despite potential sale revenue.
Selective privatisation does not establish a general response to repeated financial support. A verified current rule or clear distressed-enterprise case is needed for this precise tradeoff.
VGTRK remains a national state broadcaster; broadcasting is not left entirely to private owners.

axes.brief: Domestic procurement preferences, food self-sufficiency, strategic-investment restrictions and differential tariffs protect selected domestic production. EAEU integration and implemented Iran tariff liberalisation are important exceptions.
axes.counterEvidence: Trade barriers are selective rather than universal: preferential trade partners gain access, private imports remain important, and ordinary product taxation should not be confused with customs duties.

answers.rationale: The EAEU tariff system and 2026 higher duties on selected foreign goods protect domestic suppliers from competing imports.
Domestic procurement exclusions and food-security policy preserve barriers even where foreign goods could compete; policy does not prioritise removing most barriers regardless of domestic losses.
Resolution 1875 expressly uses domestic/EAEU preferences and restrictions, including price preferences rather than choosing solely the cheapest foreign offer.
Private import sourcing exists but origin-based duties, sanctions measures and security restrictions constrain the ability to buy solely on commercial terms.
Food-security self-sufficiency thresholds and domestic procurement restrictions prioritise national production of essential goods over unrestricted cheaper imports.

The August 2026 EEC decision independently removes titanium-scrap tariffs without requiring reciprocal foreign tariff cuts. Russia also uses reciprocal free-trade agreements and retaliatory duties, so unilateral barrier reduction is accepted selectively.

Import substitution and procurement preferences are evidenced, but a temporary infant-industry import restriction accepting higher consumer prices requires a more specific verified policy than the current sources.
Strategic controls and 2026 foreign-firm temporary administration impose nationality-specific conditions incompatible with generally equal establishment terms.
The Food Security Doctrine explicitly prioritises domestic agricultural independence and limits specified agricultural imports; this supports protecting farming capacity.
Import substitution, food-security targets and procurement preferences actively protect domestic firms instead of requiring adjustment without trade protection.
Differential duties apply to countries taking measures against Russian economic interests. This supports retaliatory tariffs, though the trigger includes sanctions as well as foreign tariff measures.

The standard VAT regime applies the same 22 percent rate to ordinary domestic supplies and imports. Special rates and exemptions depend on product category or taxpayer regime rather than a general foreign-origin product-tax penalty; customs duties are a separate instrument.

EAEU Treaty Annex 8 authorises countervailing remedies after investigation of subsidised imports causing or threatening material injury. This supports conditional restrictions, not a ban on every subsidised foreign firm.

The effective Iran agreement removes most bilateral tariffs while food-security and strategic-supply policy seek to limit dependency elsewhere. Liberalisation and dependency protection are both substantive policies.
State retention of strategic firms and nationality-specific intervention in foreign holdings show that control of strategic businesses is not freely awarded to the highest foreign investor.

Restrictions on foreign messengers and blocked foreign platforms prevent unrestricted purchase or use of foreign online services. The restrictions are Russian policy, distinct from foreign providers voluntarily withdrawing.

axes.brief: Russia uses strategic investment, directed subsidised credit, defence procurement and regulated essential prices within a predominantly monetary market economy. The central bank retains a price-stability mandate, and wages and rents generally remain contractual outside regulated sectors.
axes.counterEvidence: Wartime compulsory defence orders should not be generalised to all ordinary production.2026 overseas-transfer rules are more selective than 2022 restrictions, and crypto investment is distinct from competing domestic money.

answers.rationale: Ordinary private businesses retain commercial production decisions and SME entry support; defence orders and strategic plans are significant sector-specific exceptions.
Designated defence suppliers can be obliged to accept state orders under 275-FZ. This evidences compulsory output direction in a key industry, not universal quotas for the economy.
The central bank manages inflation through interest rates and demand, indicating generally market-set prices. Essential medicines, utility tariffs and selected price agreements qualify that default.
National industrial projects and the Project Finance Factory direct subsidised investment toward state-selected technologies and infrastructure.
Commercial expansion and closure remain market decisions in ordinary sectors, but compulsory strategic orders and subsidised priority investment deliberately alter those decisions.
Legally registered maximum medicine prices and retail mark-up controls constrain essential-goods suppliers; voluntary food-price agreements provide additional softer intervention.
SME simplification policy facilitates starting firms rather than requiring a general government demonstration of unmet production need; sector licensing remains an exception.
State-backed project finance and subsidised bank credit steer lending to national priorities, though commercial bank lending is not universally allocated by an administrative plan.

By June 2026 restrictions specifically target categories of unfriendly-country nonresidents and their transfers, while other routes have been liberalised. This is selective control, not either universal free movement or blanket approval.
The 2026 charging-infrastructure credit subsidy is an implemented example of using public funds to steer investment into a chosen industrial project.

The September 2026 digital-currency law allows regulated investment and certain external transactions but retains a domestic goods-and-services payment ban, preventing general monetary competition with the ruble.
Federal legislation sets a 27093-ruble monthly minimum from January 2026 rather than leaving the lowest wages wholly to bargaining.
Article 135 makes the employment contract and employer wage system the ordinary basis of pay within national minima and public-sector frameworks. There is no economy-wide government wage schedule.

The Bank of Russia’s independent constitutional mandate and actual inflation-targeting interest-rate framework weigh against government direction of lending and rates to implement the industrial plan. Cooperation with fiscal authorities qualifies independence.
Civil Code 682 makes residential contract rent a matter of agreement, with social/public housing and contractual protections as exceptions to general market pricing.

Ordinary activity combines private commercial decisions with strategic state programmes. Compulsory wartime defence orders are not evidence of general national production-and-distribution coordination in ordinary conditions.

axes.brief: The 2025 progressive income-tax scale,2026 family tax refund and means-tested benefits redistribute resources, while inheritance remains exempt and most working-age benefits are targeted and limited. Redistribution is real but not a comprehensive income-equalisation system.
axes.counterEvidence: Benefit floors are tied to subsistence measures and labour participation, with large categorical gaps. Property taxation exists but should not be described as a comprehensive net-wealth tax.

answers.rationale: Higher income-tax brackets and targeted child/family transfers deliberately shift disposable resources toward lower-income households, although the system does not strongly equalise all incomes.
The progressive rate schedule and targeted family refund accept using taxation to address household income differences; this is qualified by modest rates and categorical eligibility.
Indexed subsistence-based benefits and the new 2026 family refund strengthen eligible households’ floor while higher income and consumption taxes are retained.
The main child-income benefit is scaled to a regional subsistence threshold and means-tested, reflecting a basic safety net more clearly than equalising living standards broadly.
The five-tier personal-income schedule rises from 13 to 22 percent, increasing higher earners’ tax share without the very high marginal rates implied by strongest agreement.
Recent policy increased income-tax progressivity and introduced lower-income family refunds rather than generally preferring higher take-home pay despite wider inequality.
Inheritance receipts are generally exempt from personal income tax regardless of kinship; the system does not levy a large-inheritance transfer tax for income support.

Ordinary unemployment payments are time-limited, with lower ceilings after the first three months; separate family and categorical benefits qualify the proposition rather than creating indefinite unemployment support.

Higher taxes on very valuable property raise revenue while family transfers support low incomes, but there is no verified comprehensive net-wealth-to-transfer mechanism. Existing asset taxation and its limited scope support a conditional answer.

Subsistence-based benefit ceilings demonstrate modest support, but do not establish that keeping funders’ taxes lower is the reason or accepted tradeoff. Recent tax increases prevent inferring that motive automatically.
Benefits use subsistence thresholds, but the reviewed material does not establish an adequacy standard explicitly covering ordinary social participation beyond survival.
The implemented family refund and benefit indexation coexist with higher progressive and consumption taxes, weighing against a general priority for tax cuts over cash support.

The 2026 annual family payment refunds the difference between paid income tax and a 6 percent calculation to qualifying working parents with two or more children and income below 1.5 regional subsistence minima.
The five-tier income-tax schedule explicitly charges higher marginal rates as taxable earnings rise.
No current policy compensating owners to redistribute large private landholdings to land-poor recipients was verified. Allocation of unused public land would not establish this proposition.

The family payment reaches eligible working families up to 1.5 times the regional subsistence minimum, extending support beyond households below the basic-needs line, though other benefits remain tightly targeted.

axes.brief: Russia remains constitutionally secular with civil courts and marriage, while Orthodox institutions enjoy privileged access, public military worship and tax support. These dimensions are separated from personal religious belief and general traditionalism.
axes.counterEvidence: No state religion, clerical parliamentary seats or general religious veto is established. Public-school religious culture modules include parental choice and secular alternatives, although religious organisations review their content.

answers.rationale: Civil constitutional law is formally secular, but decree 809 gives Orthodoxy a special role in the state’s values framework and church–legislature cooperation influences policy. Justification is mixed rather than wholly religious or wholly separate.
Civil constitutional and statutory enactment supplies formal national law; religious teaching influences policy but is not itself an enforceable source equivalent to legislation.
Government and parliament retain lawmaking authority without a general clerical approval requirement, despite regular church consultation and limited religious review of curricular content.

Article 14 establishes secular government and no state or compulsory religion. The constitutional reference to ancestral belief in God does not designate a particular religion as the foundation of the state.

Article 87 describes knowledge of religious history/culture and permits parental choice among modules and alternatives; formal public-school teaching is not a compulsory conversion programme. Church involvement qualifies this secular approach.

There is no recognised state religion whose faith all public-school pupils must acquire; the law distinguishes cultural modules with alternatives from explicitly confessional private religious education.

State courts derive their authority from the civil constitution and laws. De facto religious coercion in Chechnya qualifies implementation but does not turn clerical rulings into the national judicial source.

The recurring parliamentary meetings provide an institutional channel for religious review and recommendations on proposed legislation; this is advisory participation rather than a required religious veto over every bill.
Organised Orthodox worship forms part of military commemorations in the main Armed Forces cathedral, contradicting a complete exclusion of worship from official public ceremonies.

Institutional worship and church access are verified, but the sources reviewed do not isolate public funding intended specifically to strengthen belief from cultural/heritage support or voluntary donations.

The Armed Forces’ official cathedral and permanent military relic display endorse Orthodox religious symbolism within a state military institutional setting, while ordinary government offices remain legally secular.
Orthodox Christmas remains a national public holiday, with additional religious holidays possible regionally; this recognises religious festivals without creating a state church.
Constitutional parliamentary composition contains no seats held automatically by religious office; church leaders address parliament by invitation rather than as ex-officio legislators.
Tax Code 381(2) specifically exempts property used for religious activity, including worship and ceremonies, beyond a general charitable-purpose exemption.
Family Code 10 makes civil registration the basis of marriage and spousal rights without religious approval.
Family-law authority belongs to civil legislation and courts; religious mediation or coercive local custom is not verified as a general legally binding religious-court jurisdiction.

axes.brief: Decree 809, restrictions on LGBT expression and gender transition, heterosexual marriage and pronatalist policy prioritise established family and moral norms. The assessment concerns state policy rather than assuming public unanimity.
axes.counterEvidence: Single parents retain social benefits, women’s employment is supported and early abortion remains formally legal despite growing obstacles. Regional dress practices and gradualism require evidence distinct from general traditionalist language.

answers.rationale: The state restricts competing social norms through traditional-values policy and censorship rather than making established customs generally open to substantial value-led change.
Decree 809 explicitly makes preservation and transmission of inherited Russian values a national-security and public-policy priority.
Single-parent households receive benefits, but official family policy and adoption rules privilege the traditional married male–female family rather than equal social recognition of all family forms.
Pronatalist state messaging and family policy encourage gender-differentiated parental expectations, qualified by continuing support for women’s employment and education.
The constitution protects marriage as a union of a man and a woman and enacted gender-transition restrictions reinforce that legal model.
Official traditional-values and family policies explicitly favour the conventional married family as the preferred social model.
Early abortion remains legal, but official pressure, clinic withdrawals and anti-abortion measures oppose social acceptance. Legal availability prevents treating this as a total national prohibition.

The state restricts nontraditional sexual content and parents select religious-culture modules, but these do not establish a general parental final veto over every school lesson conflicting with traditional sexual values.
Same-sex marriage is excluded and adoption restrictions expressly defend the traditional family model, contradicting equal recognition of same-sex adoptive parents.

Chechnya’s coercive religious practices are relevant regional context, but a current national preference on ordinary modest dress cannot be inferred from general traditional-values policy or older regional reports alone.

Legal gender-transition and LGBT-expression restrictions do not, by themselves, establish a rule about changing linguistic conventions to reflect self-identification. No sufficiently specific adopted language policy was verified; the earlier inference has been withdrawn.
Decree 809 explicitly requires intergenerational transmission of established moral values through education, youth and cultural policy.

Gender-transition and LGBT-expression restrictions impede equal recognition of people departing from established sex roles; ordinary nontraditional occupations remain possible, preventing the strongest blanket answer.

Preserving tradition does not establish a preference for gradual reform when faster change is popular. Recent restrictive legislation can itself be rapid; no specific comparative institutional-change principle was verified.
Restrictions on LGBT information and the traditional-values education framework oppose teaching diverse sexual orientations and gender identities on the proposed inclusive terms.
The values decree explicitly treats historical memory and continuity across generations as reasons to preserve customs, not solely their immediate practical utility.

axes.brief: The incumbent has accepted early medical deployment and strategic infrastructure development while retaining much stricter restrictions on GM cultivation. AI adoption and worker adaptation are supported together. A single uniform innovation attitude would obscure these sector differences.
axes.counterEvidence: Baikal exceptions retain conditions and protection elsewhere; medical devices require clinical evaluation. Healthy-person brain enhancement, cultivated meat and enhancement-specific embryo trials remain insufficiently evidenced. Older implemented vaccine policy is identified as historical evidence under the same incumbent, not a new 2026 measure.

answers.rationale: Sputnik V entered civilian use while post-registration studies were beginning. This implemented choice accepts substantial early benefits before long-term evidence, qualified by stricter policy in agriculture and other regulated domains.

The early civilian vaccine rollout contradicts a universal rule confining new technology to small trials until long-term risks are substantially known, although the government follows more restrictive rules for GM cultivation.

Law 482-FZ, effective March 2026, permits conversion of protected Baikal forest land for specified public roads and utilities where alternative sites are unavailable. This accepts habitat loss for substantial infrastructure benefits under conditions.

The incumbent registered and distributed new vaccines before long-term studies were complete, with post-registration monitoring rather than waiting for such evidence as an absolute condition of availability. Emergency context limits generalisation.

The AI strategy promotes productivity and workforce training; the implemented regulatory concept explicitly recognised changing demand for occupations and the need to adapt employment policy. Together they support adoption despite displacement, without endorsing unrestricted job losses.

The Baikal law permits specified transport and public-service development in protective forest areas when no alternative exists. Habitat protection is therefore important but does not always take priority over substantial public benefits.

Food security policy and food registration were reviewed, but neither establishes an adopted position on replacing conventional meat with cultivated meat before its long-term environmental effects are understood.

Clinical medical-device rules and neuroscience support do not specifically establish a research-only restriction for implants enhancing healthy people until long-term safety is known. Therapeutic-device approval cannot answer this enhancement-specific claim.

The adopted climate doctrine supports new technologies and energy efficiency together. It does not establish the requested priority for unproven large-scale technology over reducing material and energy consumption.

For projects subject to environmental expertise, Article 18 requires a positive expert conclusion before financing and implementation. This supports delaying projects lacking an adequate environmental assessment, with statutory exceptions and the bounded Baikal development permissions preventing an absolute answer.

Medical-device registration requires safety and effectiveness assessment, but a specific permission for healthy adults to obtain cognitive-enhancement implants on basic safety evidence was not verified.

The medical-device regime requires clinical safety and efficacy assessment, and specifically requires verified datasets for AI clinical testing before registration. This supports a qualified evidence-first position; an absolute demonstration across every patient group is not established.

Cell-product law restricts embryo-derived material and the ministry called clinical germline editing premature. These sources do not resolve controlled non-reproductive enhancement trials versus disease-prevention research, so a blanket answer would overstate the evidence.

The food-security doctrine retains a cultivation prohibition on genetically engineered plants except research, a restriction stronger than permitting widespread cultivation on early yield evidence. This supports the proposed long-term ecological precaution, without equating all GMO imports with cultivation.

The March 2026 Baikal changes permit specified roads and utilities to use protected forest land when alternatives are unavailable. This supports a qualified infrastructure priority rather than unrestricted development of all undeveloped land.

The government combines strong pre-deployment agricultural precaution with medical rollout under monitoring before long-term evidence. These implemented, domain-specific thresholds support a mixed position on a universal irreversible-risk delay rule.

axes.brief: Formal federalism retains regional constitutions, shared competences and limited tax discretion, but national constitutional supremacy and the unified public-authority system strongly centralise governance. National control of policing, education and emergency coordination are assessed separately.
axes.counterEvidence: Republic constitutions and other regional charters remain legally recognised. Regional tax rates, territorial healthcare additions and shared land competences prevent treating Russia as a legally unitary state with no regional discretion.

answers.rationale: Constitutional residual regional powers remain, but unified public authority and executive control limit protected regional dissent in practice. This supports qualified opposition rather than denying every regional power.

National constitutional institutions determine jurisdictional disputes and federal law controls federal and shared competences. The centralised political system reinforces that final national authority.
The constitution protects territorial integrity and contains no unilateral regional secession right; criminal repression of separatism reinforces rejection of a locally binding exit referendum.
Federal supremacy in national and shared competences and presidential powers to suspend incompatible regional executive acts allow national programmes to override contrary regional preferences.

Republics have their own constitutions and other regions have charters under the federal constitution. The legal protection is real but subordinate to national requirements and constrained political autonomy.
The Police Act places policing within a single centralised federal executive system rather than autonomous regional police governments.

The Budget Code assigns substantial specified tax shares directly to regions while federal taxes, national allocation rules and transfers also redistribute revenue. This is a mixed tax-sharing design, not evidence that every region keeps most of all taxes collected there.

Federal education standards and compulsory federal programmes establish the common curriculum; regional languages and selected modules add variation without permitting regions to replace the required national core.
Regional tax legislation can set specified rates and reliefs, which the Federal Tax Service publishes by region, but federal limits constrain this discretion.
The federal Labour Code establishes working hours and lawful dismissal grounds nationally. Regional labour competences do not confer a general power to override these employee protections.

Local boundaries and powers are governed through federal and regional statutes within the unified authority system. Local consultation or voting does not give residents a unilateral power to redesign the legal jurisdiction.

Resolution 2188 establishes national public-healthcare guarantees for 2026, with territorial programmes implementing them and able to add provision. National determination supplies a binding floor rather than excluding every regional addition.

Indigenous representative councils and cultural/resource protections exist, but the legal scheme places them within local and national authority rather than granting general independent territorial government through their own institutions.
The national Tax Code specifies the taxes, rate ceilings and scope of regional reliefs. Regions may vary rates only within this federally bounded competition framework.

Land, natural resources and environmental management are shared constitutional competences; regions administer local matters within federal requirements. Both levels retain authority rather than either enjoying an exclusive claim based solely on local effects.

The federal emergency-response plan provides central coordination and forces for emergencies crossing regional boundaries, within a tiered system that also assigns local and regional responsibilities.

axes.brief: Only domain-specific causal positions are inferred. Official emergency-psychology guidance explicitly combines biological stress predispositions with experience and regulation, and describes temperament as innate. The adopted women’s strategy identifies social and employment conditions behind wage disadvantage.
axes.counterEvidence: These documents do not establish a comprehensive government theory of human traits. Regional guidance has a narrower institutional scope than federal law; PTSD guidance confirms an adopted historical model but its scheduled 2025 review requires caution. Traditional values, religious policy and research funding are not treated as evidence of inherited causes.

answers.rationale: Emergency psychology describes particular stress processes and traditional-values policy prescribes conduct, but neither establishes the comparative causal weight of upbringing versus inheritance across human behaviour generally.

Neither education policy nor nationalities policy establishes an adopted explanation of national IQ-score differences in terms of inherited causes. No official comparative causal position was verified.

Pronatalist and traditional-family policies prescribe sex roles; the women’s strategy discusses social barriers. Neither settles whether behavioural differences between men and women arise mainly from social experience or biology.

Official MCHS guidance explicitly discusses innate temperament and nervous-system differences alongside psychological resources, experience and learned regulation of stress. This domain-specific interaction model supports mixed rather than exclusive biological predominance.

Occupational training and encouragement of women in higher-paid sectors demonstrate policy intervention, not an adopted conclusion that personal interests arise more from experience than inherited tendencies.

The reviewed stress and temperament guidance does not establish the relative hereditary contribution to ordinary risk-taking. Military or entrepreneurial encouragement cannot supply that causal comparison.
Nationalities integration and values education seek cooperative conduct, but do not compare social surroundings with inherited tendencies as explanations of cooperative habits.
The official stress guidance concerns emotional responses and resilience; it does not attribute differences in empathic capacity predominantly to inheritance or to upbringing.

Clinical trauma guidance includes acquired concentration symptoms, but this is insufficient to generalise about the relative causes of attention differences across the population. Research or training benefits do not resolve the comparative claim.

A programme for teaching traditional morality does not establish the causes of immediate moral intuitions. No adopted comparative explanation of biological predispositions versus culture was verified.

The adopted PTSD model explains learned trauma triggers, while current official stress guidance also recognises innate emotional vulnerability. Together these support a domain-specific interaction of experience and predisposition in perceived threat; no quantitative primacy is claimed.

MCHS psychological guidance expressly describes temperament through innate emotional programmes and nervous-system characteristics, especially apparent under extreme conditions. The qualified inference reflects the regional institutional source and does not claim all personality is inherited.

Traditional cultural policy does not determine whether attraction preferences arise predominantly from culture or inheritance; no government-adopted comparative explanation of physical attractiveness preferences was found.

Nationalities policy concerns cohesion and migration rules concern security, but neither supplies an adopted biological explanation of racial differences in violent conduct. Inferring one would conflate policy treatment with causal belief.

Official stress self-regulation guidance demonstrates learnability, but does not compare learning with inherited racial tendencies as explanations of ordinary self-control. That specific racial comparison remains unverified.

In its official CESCR reply, paragraph 63, Russia links wage differences both to traditional family divisions and associated choices of hours/intensity, then to work complexity and conditions. This explicitly combines social allocation and economic job characteristics rather than treating either as an exclusive cause.
